name: legacy-window
intent: Keep one frozen legacy interface or wire format in front of a modernized implementation, so that consumers which cannot be changed keep seeing exactly the old shape while everything behind the window moves on.
problem: A legacy client, partner or on-premise system binds to the shape it has always seen - method names, field names, fixed widths, defaults, error codes - and cannot be changed on the team's schedule. The implementation behind that contract is being replaced; touching it threatens the contract, and changing the contract breaks the caller, so the two have to be separated.
context: Applies at an integration boundary during incremental modernization: replacing a core or a vendor product, splitting a monolith, or moving from XML/EDI/fixed-width to JSON and events, while at least one consumer must keep working unchanged for a bounded period. The window is a component at that boundary, not the migration strategy itself: it owns the frozen shape and the translation to and from the new canonical model.
benefits: Consumers stay unchanged: no coordinated release with a partner, no on-premise client update, no integration freeze while the core is replaced.
The modernized core evolves under its own contract; legacy quirks - encodings, code lists, defaults, error conventions - never enter the canonical model.
Everything legacy-specific is localised in one component per contract, so it can be counted, tested and deleted instead of being smeared across the codebase.
Migration becomes incremental and reversible: the old shape keeps being served while new paths are brought online behind it.
The frozen shape can be pinned by executable fixtures - golden requests and replies replayed in CI - so 'we did not break the legacy client' becomes a check rather than an opinion.
It gives the retirement conversation an object: the window, its consumers and its expiry are named in one place.
tradeoffs: Two contracts to maintain: the legacy shape cannot evolve, so mapping code, dual DTOs and duplicated validation accumulate for as long as the window lives.

The mapping is lossy in one direction and inventive in the other: the new model expresses things the old shape cannot (defaults or truncation have to be invented), while legacy fields the new model has no place for must be dropped deliberately or carried as baggage.
Each additional legacy consumer or contract version adds a shape to keep alive; the translation matrix grows unless one shape is frozen for all of them.
Damage is easy to miss: a dropped, rounded or defaulted field produces plausible but wrong payloads instead of an error unless the mapping is total and verified against fixtures.
It preserves the weakest constraints (character sets, field widths, precision, error codes) as the effective external semantics of the modernized system.
Without an owner and an expiry the window becomes permanent, and the newest component in the estate is the legacy one.

participants.responsibility: The client, partner or component that binds to the frozen shape and cannot or will not be changed during the migration window; it is the reason the window exists.
The boundary component that exposes exactly the old contract - same signatures, names, formats, defaults and error semantics - and nothing more; it holds no business rules of its own.

Bi-directional mapping between the legacy shape and the canonical model: field and schema mapping, defaults for absent data, unit and encoding conversion, and an explicit rejection path for what cannot be represented.
The replacement implementation with its own contract and model; it must be able to serve everything the window promises and knows nothing about the legacy encoding.
Golden conversations captured from the old interface - requests, replies, error cases - replayed against the window in CI, so the frozen shape is executable rather than documentation.
Accounts for the window: tracks which consumers still need it, publishes the review or expiry date, and removes the window once the last consumer has migrated.

use_cases: A mainframe or EDI partner must keep receiving the fixed-width or X12 record it has consumed for years while the order core behind it is rebuilt as services and events.
An on-premise desktop client that cannot ship an update keeps its SOAP endpoint — same WSDL, same fault codes — while the service is rebuilt as REST/JSON internally.
A legacy nightly batch job reads a CSV extract, so the window renders the old file layout from the new event stream.
A vendor product is replaced module by module and the old module's stored-procedure and database contract stays published until the last consumer has migrated.
A public API keeps its URL paths, payload shapes and error bodies frozen for a large external client base while the backends are split into new services.
A CORBA/RMI or JMS client keeps its interface while the server is rebuilt behind a plain internal API (Service Providing Mimic).

A new logistics system captures legacy events via Event Interception — the interceptor is a Service Providing Mimic conforming to the legacy event consumption interface while the new system processes fulfilment.

A Business Performance reporting process needs logistics metrics, so a Service Consuming Mimic replicates required data into the legacy reporting database conforming to its schema and semantics — the legacy DB is unaware.
An organisation splits a monolith and routes inbound legacy traffic through the window while new services are brought online behind it, using a Strangler Fig to gradually divert flow.

Kubernetes CustomResourceDefinitions serve multiple API versions and can use a conversion webhook between served versions and a canonical storage version, preserving existing API clients while the resource model evolves.

Envoy's gRPC-JSON transcoder keeps a REST/JSON HTTP surface available while translating requests and responses to a gRPC service, isolating the internal interface from clients that still use the old protocol shape.

Apache Camel bridges existing Spring-WS endpoint mappings into Camel routes and applies its Message Translator EIP for explicit format conversion, providing a compatibility seam around legacy SOAP integrations.
avoid_when: The consumer can be changed in the same release: translate once and move everyone to the new contract - an Adapter or Message Translator at the edge, with no lifetime promise, is enough.
The consumer already tolerates change (a Tolerant Reader, or a versioned published language): the old shape does not need to be preserved verbatim.
Nothing is being replaced behind the contract: a facade or proxy without translation only adds a hop.

An external product or gateway already versions and freezes the contract for you (API gateway, broker schema registry, ESB): duplicating the freeze in application code doubles maintenance without buying anything.
The legacy shape is not actually stable - the owning team keeps editing it - because a window nobody controls will break anyway and pins the wrong contract.
anti_patterns: 'Window as the model': the modernized core starts consuming and emitting the legacy shape, so the legacy contract has spread inward and there is nothing left to retire.
'Opaque tunnel': the window forwards the legacy payload as a blob, so the old semantics - and its bugs - continue unnoticed behind a new component.
'Permanent appendage': windows created without an owner, a consumer list or an expiry date, kept forever because nobody can prove they are unused.
'One window per caller': copy-pasting the window for every consumer or contract version instead of freezing one shape and versioning it deliberately.
'New features through the old door': shipping new functionality only in the legacy shape, guaranteeing that the new contract is never adopted.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: contract and format translation is a boundary concern, never domain logic.
Open/closed: the legacy contract is closed for modification while the new core stays open for extension and change.
Information hiding: legacy quirks - encodings, code lists, defaults, error conventions - are confined to the window.
Dependency inversion: the modernized system and its new consumers depend on the new contract; only the window knows the old shape.
Encapsulate what varies: the unstable thing (the legacy format) is the thing being wrapped.
best_practices: Capture the legacy contract as executable fixtures — golden requests and replies including error and edge cases — before writing the translator, and replay them in CI. This makes 'we did not break the legacy client' a check, not an opinion.

Distinguish the two mimic subtypes: a Service Providing Mimic encapsulates a new implementation behind a legacy interface (legacy clients are unaware); a Service Consuming Mimic collaborates with legacy systems that have not yet been replaced using their existing legacy interfaces (legacy systems are unaware). Choose the right subtype based on which side cannot change.
Keep the window a pure translation layer: no business rules, no state the core should own, no caching of decisions. Business logic belongs in the Modernized Core; the window only maps shapes.

Make the mapping total and explicit: enumerate every legacy field, name the default for each absent field, and reject (with a legacy-equivalent error or dead-letter) anything that cannot be represented — never drop silently.
Freeze one contract per legacy interface rather than one window per consumer, and maintain a consumer registry so you know which interfaces are still in use and by whom.
Route the old shape through an explicit channel, route, or version prefix so that retiring the window is a routing configuration change, not a code migration.
Log mapping decisions at the boundary (field dropped, default applied, value clamped, code unknown) so drift surfaces in observability tooling rather than in a partner's complaint.
Assign a Sunset Owner for each window with a documented review or expiry date; without explicit ownership the window becomes permanent and the newest component in the estate.

Coordinate the window with the broader Transitional Architecture: the window is not the migration strategy itself but an enabler that realises seams discovered through understanding existing and target business processes.
When multiple windows exist, keep them isolated from each other; a window must not call another window to avoid chaining legacy constraints.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003), Message Translator chapter: 'Use a special filter, a Message Translator, between other filters or applications to translate one data format into another.' Describes how to connect legacy applications with proprietary data models via messaging; Channel Adapter covers connecting an application to the messaging system so it can send and receive messages.

Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns (2003), Canonical DataModel chapter: 'Design a Canonical Data Model that is independent from any specific application. Require each application to produce and consume messages in this common format.' A CDM reduces translator count from O(n²) to O(n) as applications grow.

Cartwright, Horn & Lewis, Patterns of Legacy Displacement (martinfowler.com, 2022): 'When incrementally replacing legacy systems with new ones, the new system must meet some existing (often implicit) contract, and so the new system must become a Legacy Mimic. A Legacy Mimic often realises the Anti-Corruption Layer pattern.' Introduces two subtypes: Service Providing Mimic (new system behind legacy interface) and Service Consuming Mimic (new system consuming legacy interfaces transparently to the old system).

Evans, Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software (2003) — Anti-Corruption Layer: 'Create an isolating layer to provide clients with functionality in terms of their own domain model. The layer talks to the other system through its existing interface, requiring little or no modification to the other system. Internally the layer translates in both directions as necessary between the two models.' Legacy Mimic is the transitional, expiring specialisation of this pattern.
pitfalls: Leakage inward: the Modernized Core starts consuming or emitting the legacy shape, so the legacy contract spreads into the canonical model and there is nothing left to retire — the window has failed silently.
Opaque tunnel: the window forwards the legacy payload as a blob, so old semantics and old bugs survive unexamined behind a new component name.
Mapping happy path only: absent fields, unknown codes and error replies are silently dropped or defaulted, producing plausible but wrong payloads that break clients in production.
Permanent appendage: a window created without an owner, consumer list or expiry date, kept forever because nobody can prove it is unused — the newest legacy component in the estate.
One window per consumer: copy-pasting the window for every caller instead of freezing one shape and tracking multiple consumers on it, multiplying translation maintenance.
New features through the old door: shipping new functionality only via the legacy shape to avoid disrupting consumers, guaranteeing the new contract is never adopted and the window never retires.
No golden fixtures: the window is tested against the live legacy system rather than pinned to captured request/response pairs, so regressions are discovered by the partner not by CI.
Silent rejection: unmappable payloads are discarded without a legacy-equivalent error or dead-letter, leaving the caller with a timeout and no diagnostic.
Mixing windows: two windows that call each other to chain legacy translations, turning the seam into a permanent coupling with no clear ownership or retirement path.

Wrong move: Treat the compatibility window as the migration plan -> the translation seam can outlive the replacement and become a permanent hybrid with duplicated operational cost -> instead assign an owner, consumer registry, review date and explicit removal criterion.

Wrong move: Assume protocol translation is semantic compatibility -> payloads can still parse while defaults, enum mappings, precision and error behavior drift -> instead pin golden conversations and make every lossy mapping or rejection explicit.
